title: Electrical Control of Altermagnetism in a Quasi-1D Magnet
authors: Alberto M. Ruiz, Cuiju Yu, Diego López-Alcalá, Jose L. Lado, Adolfo O. Fumega, José J. Baldoví
abstract: Altermagnetism is a collinear magnetic state characterized by momentum-dependent spin splitting in fully compensated materials. While widely investigated in systems governed by three- or two-dimensional exchange interactions, its extension to quasi-one-dimensional magnets remains almost unexplored. Focusing on the experimentally established AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ van der Waals magnet, we demonstrate that antiferromagnetic chains embedded in a two-dimensional lattice provide a general route to altermagnetism. Combining first-principles calculations and spin-space-group analysis, we show that out-of-plane symmetry breaking can generate a nonrelativistic d-wave spin splitting. An external out-of-plane electric field validates this mechanism, where the induced splitting increases linearly with field strength and reverses sign with field direction. We rationalize such behaviour by constructing an effective tight-binding model, which links the altermagnetic response to anisotropic third-neighbor interchain hoppings. Additionally, we show that Janus substitution also induces a d-wave spin texture, while ferroelectric interfacing with CuInP$_2$S$_6$ enables polarization-controlled spin-split bands in a fully compensated ferrimagnetic state. Our results establish quasi-one-dimensional antiferromagnets as building blocks for altermagnetism.
summary: This work establishes $	ext{AgCrP}_2	ext{S}_6$ as a novel platform for studying altermagnetism in quasi-1D magnets. By applying an out-of-plane electric field, the authors demonstrate electrical control over the magnetic state, inducing a measurable d-wave spin splitting. This mechanism is further generalized using chemical and ferroelectric interfaces to achieve polarization-controlled magnetism.
main_problem: The study aims to extend the understanding of altermagnetism, a momentum-dependent spin splitting, from 2D/3D systems to quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) magnets and demonstrate its electrical control.
main_result: The authors show that an out-of-plane electric field can induce a nonrelativistic d-wave altermagnetic spin texture in $	ext{AgCrP}_2	ext{S}_6$, which is also controllable via chemical substitution or ferroelectric interfaces.
method: The research combines first-principles calculations (DFT) with symmetry analysis and the construction of an effective tight-binding model to rationalize the magnetic response.
model_or_system: The primary system is monolayer $	ext{AgCrP}_2	ext{S}_6$, which features quasi-1D antiferromagnetic chains coupled in a 2D lattice. The control mechanisms involve applying external electric fields, performing Janus substitutions, or interfacing with ferroelectric materials.
key_observables: Momentum-dependent spin splitting magnitude (up to $32 	ext{ meV}$), sign reversal of the splitting upon field reversal, and confirmation of a d-wave texture in the band structure.
important_parameters: Out-of-plane electric field strength ($E_{\perp}$), anisotropic third-neighbor interchain hopping ($\delta t$), and polarization state (e.g., up-up vs. down-down).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on DFT calculations and effective tight-binding models, focusing specifically on the symmetry-allowed ferromagnetic interchain alignment for altermagnetism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural changes under electric fields, showing band structures that transition from spin-degenerate to exhibit a d-wave spin splitting dependent on field polarity. Momentum maps confirm the d-wave nature of the texture.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by analyzing symmetry requirements for altermagnetism in quasi-1D systems. It then details the electrical control mechanism using $	ext{AgCrP}_2	ext{S}_6$ under an external field, followed by extensions to chemical (Janus) and interfacial engineering with ferroelectrics.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of electrically controlling spin splitting via symmetry breaking is highly relevant to quantum materials research that seeks electrical control over quantum states, bridging concepts from spintronics and topological physics.
